paragraphs.text: The leaf comes from [Zhenghe](zhenghe:where-it-is), an inland mountain county in the north of Fujian. It sits back from the coast under forest and mist, and its winters are colder than on the coastal tea hills. With Fuding it is one of the two main homes of white tea. The county grows its own bush, [Zhenghe Da Bai](zhenghe:known-for), which is said to have been found at Tieshan in the late nineteenth century and is now planted well beyond the area.

[White tea](white:definition) is made in the fewest steps. The leaf is [withered and then dried at low heat](fujian-white:making), and it is never fixed or rolled. This one was pressed into a cake. Dated 2008, it comes from the early years of [pressed white tea](fujian-white:cakes). Cakes began in the 2000s and spread around 2010, because a cake is easier to keep and carry than loose leaf. Some cakes were pressed from leaf that had already aged loose, so the year can mark the pressing rather than the pick.

At eighteen years the cake is well past the seven of the trade's saying, [tea in the first year, medicine at three, a treasure at seven](fujian-white:ageing). That is a saying, not a tested claim, and no agreed number of years makes a white tea aged. The years change the liquor too, which deepens and reddens as the tea ages.

brewing.text: Gongfu style, use about 1 gram of leaf to 15 to 25 ml of water, for example 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan; weigh it, since the leaf is light and bulky. Silver Needle and young, delicate tea take water below the boil, about 75 to 90°C; older, leafier or aged tea takes water at or near the boil. Start with a steep of 10 to 45 seconds and add a few seconds each round. An aged cake is often rinsed quickly first, and older pressed tea can be simmered on the stove, about 5 grams to 500 ml for 3 to 10 minutes; young, delicate tea is not.

notice.text: Jujube or dried dates, herbs and medicine, wood, honey and dried fruit, a deeper, redder liquor, a thicker, rounder body, and less lift in the scent than a young tea.
